verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,
“Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem;
and say to them, Yahweh, the God of Israel says: ‘Cursed is the man who doesn’t hear the words of this covenant,

which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace,’ saying, ‘Obey my voice, and do them, according to all which I command you: so you shall be my people, and I will be your God;
that I may establish the oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey,’ as it is today.” Then answered I, and said, “Amen, Yahweh.”
Yahweh said to me, “Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying, ‘Hear the words of this covenant, and do them.
For I earnestly protested to your fathers in the day that I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, even to this day, rising early and protesting, saying, “Obey my voice.”

Yet they didn’t obey, nor turn their ear, but walked everyone in the stubbornness of their evil heart: therefore I brought on them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they didn’t do them.’”
Yahweh said to me, “A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words; and they are gone after other gods to serve them: the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers.
Therefore Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on them, which they shall not be able to escape; and they shall cry to me, but I will not listen to them.
Then shall the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem go and cry to the gods to which they offer incense: but they will not save them at all in the time of their trouble.

For according to the number of your cities are your gods, Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have you set up altars to the shameful thing, even altars to burn incense to Baal.’
“Therefore don’t pray for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them; for I will not hear them in the time that they cry to me because of their trouble.
What has my beloved to do in my house, since she has worked lewdness with many, and the holy flesh is passed from you? When you do evil, then you rejoice.”
Yahweh called your name, “A green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit.” With the noise of a great tumult he has kindled fire on it, and its branches are broken.

For Yahweh of Armies, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you, because of the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have worked for themselves in provoking me to anger by offering incense to Baal.
Yahweh gave me knowledge of it, and I knew it: then you showed me their doings.

But I was like a gentle lamb that is led to the slaughter; and I didn’t know that they had devised devices against me, saying, “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered.”
But, Yahweh of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind, I shall see your vengeance on them; for to you I have revealed my cause.
“Therefore Yahweh says concerning the men of Anathoth, who seek your life, saying, ‘You shall not prophesy in Yahweh’s name, that you not die by our hand;’
therefore Yahweh of Armies says, ‘Behold, I will punish them: the young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine;
and there shall be no remnant to them: for I will bring evil on the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation.’”

footnotes.content: Jeremiah receives his marching orders—the word of the Lord comes to him with a message about a covenant. That quiet opening, 'the word that came to Jeremiah,' reminds us how God speaks into the silence of a faithful heart. We too are given words to speak, if we're listening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah is told to hear the words of the covenant first—and then to speak them. There's wisdom in that order: we can't truthfully carry a word we haven't truly heard. The covenant belongs to God first, to us, to our neighbors in that order.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A curse falls on the man who doesn't hear the covenant words. But notice: the curse is for refusing to hear, not for stumbling once you've heard. God's law invites us to listen closely. Jesus would later say, 'Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command echoes back to Exodus—'out of the iron furnace' of Egypt. God had freed them with a mighty hand, asking only obedience in return. The pattern holds: He rescues us first, then invites us to follow. Grace precedes law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The promise shimmers like honey over milk—abundance, security, a good land. And Jeremiah answers 'Amen,' as if to say, 'Yes, Lord, I see it. I believe it.' Even in exile and hardship ahead, that 'Amen' holds fast. We too can say yes to God's promise even when we can't yet see the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God sends Jeremiah to the cities, the streets—the real places where real people live. There's no hiding behind closed doors or empty ritual. True proclamation goes where the people are, with words they can hear and choose to obey or refuse.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God emphasizes His faithfulness: 'rising early and protesting.' He didn't give up on them. He kept sending the message, kept calling them back. Our own stubborn hearts know that kind of patient love—the Lord's voice calling us awake, day after day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They wouldn't obey or turn their ear. Instead they walked in 'stubbornness of their evil heart'—choosing themselves over the covenant. And so the covenant's words, meant to bless, became judgment instead. We see in their refusal the shape of all rejection: turning away from light brings darkness, not escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A conspiracy is uncovered—not a secret rebellion in a foreign court, but a hidden alliance in God's own city, Jerusalem. Sometimes the deepest betrayals come from those closest to us, those we've loved and taught. Jeremiah feels that sting keenly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They didn't invent their idolatry—they 'turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers.' Sin has a long memory, passed like a bitter inheritance from hand to hand. Yet the cross breaks that chain. In Jesus, our sins need not echo forward to our children.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word comes hard: God will bring evil on them, and they won't escape it. They'll cry out, but He won't listen. It sounds like the opposite of His nature until we see it truly—a father's grief over those who've chosen darkness. Love that never stops caring must sometimes allow consequences.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In their trouble, they'll cry to the gods they've made—gods who 'will not save them at all.' Here's a piercing truth: the idols we chase when we're healthy desert us entirely when we're desperate. Only the true God stays faithful to the broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There are as many gods and altars in Jerusalem as there are cities and streets—abundance of false worship, poverty of true faith. The image is darkly comic: they've paved their city with idolatry. Yet God sees it and grieves, still holding out His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The most difficult word: Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them. Not because God doesn't love them, but because their refusal has reached a point where intercession itself would enable further hardening. Sometimes we must let others bear the weight of their own choice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God calls them His 'beloved'—and the wound in that word is terrible. She was meant to be His, faithful and fair, but she's defiled herself. He sees her folly and it breaks Him. There's tenderness even in judgment when it comes from a heart that loved first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God had called them 'a green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit'—a tender name for what they were meant to be. Now He Himself has kindled a fire on it, and the branches break. Sometimes judgment comes from the One who planted you, because He alone knows the full scope of what was wasted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord of Armies, who planted them, pronounces evil against them. They provoked Him by offering to Baal what belonged only to Him. There's a ferocity in God's love—He will not share His people with a lie, not because He's jealous like us, but because He knows what false gods truly cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord shows Jeremiah what the people are doing—a terrible gift of sight. To know their plots is to bear the weight of their intention. Jeremiah carries the knowledge of their hatred, knowing what's coming. We who follow Jesus know this too: He saw His killers and loved them anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo of the Lamb of God, the true Innocent led to slaughter. Jeremiah's image of himself—'a gentle lamb led to slaughter'—shapes how we see Jesus centuries later. Both spoke truth; both were hunted for it. Both trusted the Father's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the midst of the plot against him, Jeremiah appeals to the 'Yahweh of Armies, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and mind.' He doesn't plead for escape—he asks for vindication. He trusts the One who sees not just deeds but the true bent of the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Anathoth, Jeremiah's own village, seek his death. They want him silenced—no more prophecy in Yahweh's name. It's a bitter irony: he was born there, knew those faces, and they've turned on him. Yet he won't stop speaking what he's been given to say.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's word against Anathoth is swift and terrible: the young men shall fall by the sword, sons and daughters by famine. This is what happens when you raise your hand against the Lord's messenger. There is no safety in that choice, only judgment that will echo through generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not a remnant shall be left to them—the visitation comes complete. It's a hard word, final in its way, yet it serves the larger purpose: the Lord defends His prophet and guards His word. Justice will have its day, even when the righteous suffer first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
